excerpt: Commercial carpet hot-water extraction is priced per sq ft, per hour, or as an amortized monthly program, and the unit you choose changes the total more than the vendor does. This guide lays out national US ranges, minimum charges, production rates, and a worked budget for a mid-size office.
quickAnswer: Commercial carpet hot-water extraction runs about $0.09–$0.18 per sq ft per event on a contracted quarterly program, which equals $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft per month amortized, and $0.18–$0.32 per sq ft for one-off jobs. Hourly specialty billing ranges from $55–$95 per technician hour, and most vendors set a project minimum of roughly $175–$295 to cover mobilization and drying equipment.

blocks.text: Hot-water extraction, often called steam cleaning, injects heated solution into carpet fibers under pressure and immediately recovers it with vacuum. For commercial offices, it is the restorative step that removes embedded soil that nightly vacuuming and spot cleaning leave behind. Vendors price it three ways: per sq ft of carpet extracted, per technician hour, or as an amortized monthly program inside the janitorial contract. Each unit can be fair; problems arise when bids use different units or different square footage assumptions.

blocks.text: Production Rates Behind the Unit Price

Unit prices trace back to how many sq ft a technician extracts per hour. Portable heated extractors typically cover 400–700 sq ft per hour in open-plan offices, including pre-vacuum, pre-spray dwell, extraction passes, and grooming. Truck-mounted units can reach 900–1,500 sq ft per hour in large open areas but need hose runs, parking access, and building approval. At $55–$95 per hour and roughly 600 sq ft per hour, the math lands near $0.09–$0.16 per sq ft, consistent with program pricing. Furniture moving, cubicle legs, and chair mats drop production sharply, which is why one-off jobs carry higher unit prices.

blocks.title: Benchmark: program vs. one-off
blocks.text: A quarterly program at $0.09–$0.18 per sq ft per event is usually 40–50 percent cheaper per sq ft than a one-off extraction because soil levels stay low, pre-spray needs are lighter, and the vendor can schedule crews efficiently.
Worked Budget: 14,000 Sq Ft Office With 9,500 Sq Ft of Carpet

Assume a 14,000 sq ft office with 9,500 sq ft of carpet tile and the rest in VCT and tile. The tenant wants quarterly full extraction plus monthly traffic-lane extraction on 2,000 sq ft of corridors and entry zones.

blocks.caption: Annual carpet extraction budget for 9,500 sq ft of office carpet

blocks.text: Compare that monthly figure with the amortized benchmark: 9,500 sq ft at $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft per month equals $285–$570 for full extraction alone. The interim lane program accounts for the rest. If a vendor quotes a monthly deep floor program well below $0.03 per sq ft, ask how many events per year the price actually covers.

Equipment matters because under-powered machines leave carpet wet, and wet carpet wicks soil back up and can trigger odor or mildew complaints. For quarterly contract work, the Sandia Sniper 6-gallon heated extractor pairs a 100 PSI pump with dual vacuum motors and a 2000W heater, which helps keep dry times within a typical overnight window. For upholstery, chair seats, and isolated spots, the Karcher Puzzi 8/1 C, a 21.6 lb spray extractor with a 2.1-gal tank and single-stage vacuum, is built for fast-dry spot work. Between extraction events, the Oreck Commercial 550MC Orbiter, a 24 lb oscillating machine with a 13-in pad, can run low-moisture encapsulation pads on traffic lanes and also scrub tile grout in adjoining areas.

items: Ask for target dry times of 4–8 hours and confirm air movers are included for overnight jobs.
Verify the vendor follows carpet manufacturer warranty requirements, which often call for hot-water extraction at defined intervals.
Request neutral or low-residue rinse agents so carpet does not resoil quickly after cleaning.
Confirm whether furniture moving is included or billed hourly.

blocks.text: Extraction chemicals, especially pre-sprays and spotters, fall under OSHA Hazard Communication rules, so vendors should keep Safety Data Sheets on site. Slip hazards from wet carpet transitions onto hard floors are a liability concern, which is why a certificate of insurance with at least $1 million per occurrence general liability is standard. Green Seal certified pre-sprays are widely available and rarely raise unit pricing.

blocks.title: Scope exclusions to check
blocks.text: Many extraction quotes exclude moving desks or file cabinets, treating permanent stains such as ink or bleach spots, and carpet repair. Ask that these exclusions be listed explicitly so they do not appear later as surprise charges.

faqs.q: What is a fair per-sq-ft price for commercial carpet extraction?
faqs.a: On a quarterly contract program, $0.09–$0.18 per sq ft per event is typical nationally. One-off or annual jobs run $0.18–$0.32 per sq ft because soil is heavier and the vendor cannot plan crew routes. City labor rates can push both ranges higher.

faqs.q: How is extraction priced inside a monthly janitorial contract?
faqs.a: Vendors often amortize quarterly extraction at $0.03–$0.06 per sq ft per month. For 10,000 sq ft of carpet, that is $300–$600 per month added to the base janitorial price.

faqs.q: Why do small offices pay a minimum charge?
faqs.a: Mobilization, equipment loading, and drying setup cost the same regardless of area. Most vendors set a minimum of about $175–$295 per job, so a 1,000 sq ft suite pays the minimum rather than the per-sq-ft rate.

faqs.q: How long does carpet take to dry after extraction?
faqs.a: With properly powered equipment and air movers, commercial carpet tile typically dries in 4–8 hours. Glue-down broadloom in humid conditions may take longer. Schedule extraction for Friday nights or before long weekends when possible.

faqs.q: Does carpet extraction affect my carpet warranty?
faqs.a: Many commercial carpet manufacturers require periodic hot-water extraction to keep warranties valid. Keep vendor work tickets with dates and areas cleaned as documentation.
